subject: fit independent models in one go to assess prior influence

messages.author: b37012f8f028bd32
messages.subject: fit independent models in one go to assess prior influence
parts:
Dears
I would like to fit 4 different regression lines to the same data. Each regression line has a different prior for the sigma parameter:
Uniform(0,uppersigma)
with uppersigma being 5, 10, 50, and 1000
The true sigma is 5. My aim is to show 4 histograms of the 4 posterior distributions of sigma. From this plot we should see that the posterior based on the prior Unif(0,5) is constraint, whereas we get nice posterior distributions when the upper limit of the prior is larger than the upper tail of the posterior.
 
When I use uppersigma=c(10, 20, 50, 1000), I get a good fit for all 4 models, but the 4 posteriors for sigma look very similar... When I specify one of the uppersigma-values to be lower than 8, so that it constrains the posterior of sigma, the fit of ALL 4 models becomes very bad (very low neffs, high Rhat values) and all 4 posteriors for sigma are bimodal with one mass close to zero and the other mass close to the uppersigma value.  Obviously, the choice of the uppersigma for one regression line influences the fit of all the other regression lines, even if (I think) I specified 4 independent regression lines (model code below).

Isn't it possible to fit 4 independent regression lines to the same data in one go?
Before, I fitted 20 independent regression lines with different priors for the slope parameter and this seemed to work nicely. But maybe this was wrong too?
The R-Code to simulate the data and fit the model below using rstan is attached.
Thanks in advance!
Fränzi


// Normal linear regressions with varying
// priors for sigma to assess
// the influence of the prior for sigma

data {
  int<lower=0> n;
  vector[n] y;
  vector[n] x;
  vector[4] uppersigma;
}
parameters {
  vector[4] beta0;
  vector[4] beta1;
  real<lower=0> sigma[4];
}
model {
  //priors
  beta0 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta1 ~ normal(0,10);
  for(k in 1:4){
    sigma[k] ~ uniform(0,uppersigma[k]);
    // likelihood
    y ~ normal(beta0[k] + beta1[k] * x, sigma[k]);
  }
}

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fit independent models in one go to assess prior influence
parts:
Hi, Franzi.  I just have a couple comments.  First, as Bob C. knows, I really don’t like uniform priors (except for parameters with natural constraints such as correlations which are bounded between -1 and 1).  I much prefer soft constraints to hard constraints, both for computational and statistical reasons (the folk theorem comes in here).  Second, I don’t see why there would be a problem to fit 4 regression models in one go.  You just have to define all 4 sets of parameters in the model.
A

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fit independent models in one go to assess prior influence
parts:
The problem is that the variance parameters sigmas aren't constrained to the corresponding uniform intervals. Ie. the samper will generate sigma's from the interval [0,Inf] and then if sigma[k] > uppersigma[k] the sampling statement uniform(0,uppersigma[k]) will increase the log-posterior by -Infinity.

So I think there are two possibilies:
a) use different prior as Andrew suggested
b) declare 4 sigmas in the form of real<lower=0,upper=uppersigma> sigma

parts:
Dear all
thank you very much for your answers! Thanks to Herra, I feel that I have a vague imagination of the reason why my model fit failed. And thanks to Andrew and Bob, I am now playing around with folded t-distributions using the code below. Seems to work nicely, but I have to figure out a good parameterization.
It is fun - much more fun than playing with the Uniform priors that are really quite unnaturall!
Any comment about the code below is welcome (think there may be more efficient ways to code this model?).
Best
Fränzi

// priors for sigma to assess
// the influence of the prior for sigma

data {
  int<lower=0> n;
  vector[n] y;
  vector[n] x;

vector[4] priorparsigma; // parameters for folded t dist
}

parameters {
  real beta0;
  real beta1;
  real eta;
  real<lower=0> g;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  sigma <- fabs(eta)/g;

}

model {
  //priors
  beta0 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta1 ~ normal(0,10);

eta ~ normal(priorparsigma[1], priorparsigma[2]);
  g ~ gamma(priorparsigma[3], priorparsigma[4]);

  // likelihood
  y ~ normal(beta0 + beta1 * x, sigma);

}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fit independent models in one go to assess prior influence
parts:
I'd like to hear from Andrew on the applied stats part
of this. I include some comments on the computational
part of the operation below.

On Jun 16, 2014, at 3:19 PM, f ko <fraenzi...@oikostat.ch> wrote:

> Dear all
> thank you very much for your answers! Thanks to Herra, I feel that I have a vague imagination of the reason why my model fit failed. And thanks to Andrew and Bob, I am now playing around with folded t-distributions using the code below. Seems to work nicely, but I have to figure out a good parameterization.
> It is fun - much more fun than playing with the Uniform priors that are really quite unnaturall!

The tighter the priors are (up to a point), the easier time
the model will have of fitting. It'll control long excursions
into undesirable regions of the parameter space, often without
changing the posterior means in a noticeable way.
> Any comment about the code below is welcome (think there may be more efficient ways to code this model?).
See below.

> Best
> Fränzi
>
> // priors for sigma to assess
> // the influence of the prior for sigma
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> n;
> vector[n] y;
> vector[n] x;
> vector[4] priorparsigma; // parameters for folded t dist
> }
>
> parameters {
> real beta0;
> real beta1;
> real eta;
> real<lower=0> g;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> sigma <- fabs(eta)/g;
> }
>

You almost never want to use absolute values with HMC.
The problem is that it introduces two modes, at eta and
-eta. Instead, it's better here to put a constraint on
eta:

real<lower=0> eta;

But, if you have

> eta ~ normal(priorparsigma[1], priorparsigma[2]);
> g ~ gamma(priorparsigma[3], priorparsigma[4]);
then this isn't equivalent unless priorparsigma[1] = 0.

> model {
> //priors
> beta0 ~ normal(0,10);
> beta1 ~ normal(0,10);

I'd only use parameters this diffuse if you expect values
for beta0 and beta1 with absolute values above 10.
If the posterior is concentrated around a much smaller
region, then you can reduce the scale of the priors without
affecting the posterior much at all. And it'll be much
faster to converge and mix better.

- Bob
